clue.text: One diamond for the game

parts.note: a diamond is the infield of the American bat-and-ball sport, so the game played on one is wanted

explanation.surface: A single gem staked on a card or betting game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diamond' pulls towards jewels or the card suit, but here it is the square infield with four bases on which this American sport is played.
explanation.definitionFit: The playing area of this American bat-and-ball sport is called the diamond.

clue.text: Hurry at the back there, Madam !

definitions.meaning: a padded frame worn under a Victorian skirt to puff it out behind

explanation.surface: A shop assistant urges a lady to hurry along at the back of the queue.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is playful: the Victorian dress padding sat at the back of a lady's skirt.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to rush about fussily and a padded pad worn behind under a woman's skirt in Victorian fashion.

clue.text: Rents raised a pound — it's vicious !

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word turns its letters to read upwards, so they are reversed

parts.note: rents as in tears means rips
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A tenant protests that a pound added to the rent is wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns RIPS into SPIR; add A and L. 'Rents' looks like money paid to a landlord, but it means tears.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicious spiral is the stock phrase for a worsening cycle, so the clue's exclamation describes the coil itself.

clue.text: One of the big company combines that are divinely aided

definitions.text: One of the big company combines that are divinely aided

parts.words: One of the big company combines that are divinely aided
parts.note: plays on the saying that God is on the side of the big army units; 'company' and 'combines' read as business words but are military

explanation.surface: Divine help seems to favour the large business conglomerates.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'Providence is always on the side of the big battalions' is behind it; 'company' is a military unit, not a firm.
explanation.definitionFit: A large army unit made up of several companies, said in the old proverb to enjoy divine favour.

clue.text: An unlucky break

parts.note: smashing a mirror is said to bring seven years' bad luck, so the break of this object is unlucky

explanation.surface: A stroke of misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' reads as a stroke of luck, but it is literal: the superstition says breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old word for a mirror, whose breaking is held to be unlucky.

clue.text: A bad cigar, about a pound, has a distinctive flavour

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go about, around, the pound sign
a bad cigar is one that has gone wrong, so its letters are put in a new order

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A poor cigar costing about a quid has a strong taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges CIGAR to GARIC, and 'about' puts L inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The bulb is famous for its pungent taste in cooking.

clue.text: Confound with a heavy blow

parts.note: a bash is a hard blow

explanation.surface: Someone is knocked senseless by a hard hit.
explanation.definitionFit: To confound someone is to disconcert or embarrass them.

clue.text: But Browning wasn't bumped off on his

definitions.text: But Browning wasn't bumped off on his

parts.words: But Browning wasn't bumped off on his
parts.note: Robert Browning wrote 'The ... Together', while a gangster's victim taken for a final drive is murdered

explanation.surface: A remark that the poet Browning was not murdered on some trip of his.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Browning, the Victorian poet, wrote 'The Last Ride Together'; in gangster slang the victim is taken on a final drive and killed, which Browning's lover's outing was not.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both Browning's poem title and gangland slang for a victim's final journey.

clue.text: Lowers their charges

parts.note: lowers read as 'things that low', that is moo, are the cattle in the care of these herdsmen

explanation.surface: Someone cuts their prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lowers' reads as reduces, but it is low-ers, animals that moo; 'charges' are those in someone's care, not fees.
explanation.definitionFit: Cattle that moo are the animals these herdsmen look after.

clue.text: Once a common target for public marksmanship

definitions.text: Once a common target for public marksmanship

parts.words: Once a common target for public marksmanship
parts.note: marksmanship here is aiming saliva at a receptacle in a pub or public place, as men once did

explanation.surface: A remark about an old shooting-range target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marksmanship' suggests firearms, but the aim is with spit; 'public' hints at the pub, where the receptacle stood.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowl once provided in pubs and public rooms for people to spit into.

clue.text: Hostilities observed in the City

parts.note: hostilities are wars
observed means saw

explanation.surface: Fighting is seen in a town.
explanation.definitionFit: The Polish capital is a city.

clue.text: Puts briefly in perspective

parts.note: drawing a thing in perspective makes it look shorter along the line of sight; 'briefly' suggests summarising

explanation.surface: Someone sums up a situation with a quick sense of proportion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puts briefly' sounds like summarising, but in drawing an object receding from the viewer is shortened to show depth.
explanation.definitionFit: In art, drawing something in perspective so that it appears shorter as it recedes.

clue.text: Beast of burden of many a Buddhist monk

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword stand-in for many
a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist monk

explanation.surface: The pack animal owned by many a Buddhist monk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'many' is L, the Roman fifty, placed before LAMA.
explanation.definitionFit: The South American animal is used to carry loads.

clue.text: A smoother runner on the rails

definitions.text: A smoother runner on the rails

parts.words: A smoother runner on the rails
parts.note: a smoother is a flat-iron and a runner is a horse, together an old name for a locomotive

explanation.surface: Something that glides more easily along the track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoother' reads as a comparative, but it is a noun: a flat-iron. Put it with a horse and you have the old nickname for a steam engine.
explanation.definitionFit: An old poetic name for a railway locomotive.

clue.text: Unassisted, like Captain Hook

definitions.meaning: Peter Pan's enemy lost a hand to the crocodile and has only one

explanation.surface: Someone managed it alone, like the pirate in Peter Pan.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means done without help and also having only one hand, as the hook-handed pirate captain does.

clue.text: Sum for expenses of repairing the ocean wall

indicators.note: repairing means the letters of ocean wall are put back together in a new order

explanation.surface: Money set aside to mend the sea wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repairing' rearranges OCEAN WALL; 'the' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An amount of money given regularly to cover costs.

clue.text: What a couple of chumps taking in a killer!

indicators.note: a couple of means the word for chumps is written twice

parts.note: an ass is a fool, a chump

explanation.surface: Two fools take in a murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What' and 'taking' are link words; 'chumps' looks like the subject of the sentence but is only the fodder, used twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A murderer, especially one hired to kill a prominent person.

clue.text: Lug along a historian as interpreter

parts.note: to lug is to drag
Sir Charles Oman was a British military historian

explanation.surface: A scholar is hauled along to act as translator.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Charles Oman wrote the history of the Peninsular War.
explanation.definitionFit: A guide and translator in Arabic-, Turkish- or Persian-speaking countries.

clue.text: Its victim seeks vainly for inspiration

definitions.text: Its victim seeks vainly for inspiration

parts.words: Its victim seeks vainly for inspiration
parts.note: inspiration is breathing in; someone held by the throat cannot draw breath

explanation.surface: A writer hunts in vain for an idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiration' suggests a creative spark, but it is literal breathing in, denied to someone gripped round the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: A grip round the neck that stops someone breathing.

clue.text: Sounds like a young pen-friend written to in Scotland

indicators.note: says that the word for a young swan is heard, not spelt

parts.note: a pen is a female swan; a young one, a friend of the pen, is a cygnet

explanation.surface: A child corresponding with a pen pal in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland, solicitors are Writers to the Signet, so the seal is what they write to. 'Pen-friend' is not a correspondent: a pen is a female swan.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers to the Signet are a Scottish society of solicitors, named for the royal seal.

clue.text: Popular count ?

parts.note: popular here means of the populace, and count is a tally, not a nobleman

explanation.surface: A well-loved nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular count' looks like a beloved aristocrat, but it is a count of the population.
explanation.definitionFit: An official count of a country's population.

clue.text: Is it gross rage that makes him one ?

definitions.text: Is it gross rage that makes him one ?

indicators.note: the letters of gross rage make up, rearranged, the word for the person

explanation.surface: Asks whether extreme anger is what turns a man into an attacker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' rearranges GROSS RAGE, and the whole clue says what drives such a person.
explanation.definitionFit: One who attacks first is driven by violent anger.

clue.text: Consume about a hundred and fifty with conspicuous success

indicators.note: the word for consume goes about, around, the Roman numerals

parts.note: to consume food is to eat
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred and L for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone eats about a hundred and fifty and is a great hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals the container; the Roman numerals for the number go inside the verb for consume.
explanation.definitionFit: Brilliant success or acclaim, a word borrowed from French.

clue.text: It's great, this way, for New Yorkers

definitions.text: It's great, this way, for New Yorkers

parts.words: It's great, this way, for New Yorkers
parts.note: New Yorkers call Broadway the Great ___ Way, after its bright lights

explanation.surface: Someone says this route is wonderful for people in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadway in New York is nicknamed the Great White Way; the missing middle word is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The colour word completes the nickname of Broadway, the Great White Way.

clue.text: Herb isn't very intelligent

definitions.meaning: an old word for a medicinal plant
one who is not bright is said to be this, slow-witted

explanation.surface: A man called Herb is not very bright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' looks like a man's name, the subject of the sentence, but it is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old name for a medicinal herb, and describes someone of low intelligence.

clue.text: Write numbers within our range

parts.note: to write is to pen
nines are numbers

explanation.surface: Someone writes figures within limits.
explanation.walkthrough: THE PENNINES are the hill range forming the backbone of northern England; 'our' speaks as a British paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The chain of hills running down northern England, called 'our' range by a British setter.

clue.text: And this number's in excellent shape

annotationWithheld.why: And this number's in excellent shape (6): the number is the answer, but no reading found ties 'in excellent shape' to it, so the cryptic sense cannot be explained honestly
annotationWithheld.clue: And this number's in excellent shape

clue.text: It's best to take nothing into a vessel as a fire precaution

indicators.note: into means the best and nothing are put inside the ship abbreviation

parts.note: SS is a steamship
taken as written
O is the shape of zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Advice that the safest course is to put nothing aboard a ship to avoid fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's best' reads as advice, but 'best' is only fodder; 'into' signals the container, with the ship holding both best and nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The mineral fibre was used in fireproofing because it does not burn.
